planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in mid to late spring once soil has warmed, in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; wait until nighttime lows are reliably above 50F before planting out.

directions: Hammock fern forms a low, spreading colony of once-pinnate fronds that emerge a striking salmon-pink to coppery-rose before maturing to rich medium green, giving it seasonal color rarely seen among garden ferns. Native to hammocks and moist woodland understories from Mexico through the Caribbean and naturalized in Florida, it spreads by creeping rhizomes to form an attractive small-scale groundcover in consistently moist, humus-rich shade. In the Gulf Coast garden it performs best at the warmer end of its range, tolerating summer heat and humidity with ease but benefiting from heavy mulch or container culture where hard freezes threaten. Combine with other warm-climate ferns and broadleaf evergreens in a sheltered courtyard or shaded bed out of drying winter winds.
sources: US Fish and Wildlife Service Species Profile
Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions or rooted plantlets in spring in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from cold, drying winds; mulch the crown heavily in autumn where winters approach the cold edge of its range.

directions: Oriental chain fern is a bold, arching evergreen fern whose broad, glossy, pinnate to bipinnate fronds emerge coppery orange in spring before maturing to deep green, eventually reaching four feet tall and wide or more where winters stay mild. Small plantlets form along the mature fronds and root readily where they touch soil, so gardeners can propagate new plants simply by pegging a frond tip down or removing rooted offsets in autumn. Best sited in partial to full shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil, it takes the heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer in stride but appreciates a dry winter mulch at the cooler edge of its range. Its coarse, tropical texture makes a strong architectural counterpoint to fine-textured Dryopteris and Athyrium plantings in a warm-climate shade border.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; established plants tolerate brief dry spells and coastal salt exposure better than most ferns.

directions: Butterfield's holly fern is a rare selection of Japanese holly fern distinguished by long, arching, glossy dark-green fronds with unusually deep, sharply serrated leaflet margins, giving the whole clump a jagged, textural look unlike the smoother-edged species. Like the straight species, it is remarkably tolerant of heat, salt spray, and dry shade once established, making it one of the toughest broadleaf evergreen ferns for difficult sites along the Gulf Coast. Site it in part to full shade in well-drained soil, where its stiff, leathery fronds resist wind damage and provide months of structural evergreen interest with minimal upkeep. Use it as a specimen near entries and shaded patios where its distinctive serrated foliage can be appreciated up close.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
JC Raulston Arboretum at NC State University

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in evenly moist, humus-rich woodland soil in partial to full shade; this sterile hybrid must be propagated by division rather than spores, since it does not come true and rarely sets viable spores.

directions: 'Stableri' is a vigorous, semi-evergreen hybrid shield fern combining the sturdy, golden-scaled fronds of Dryopteris affinis with the finely cut, lacy texture of Dryopteris filix-mas, producing narrow, upright, slightly crisped fronds to three or four feet from an erect, vase-shaped crown. New fiddleheads unfurl covered in coppery-gold scales that persist along the stipes as the dark green fronds mature, adding textural interest through the growing season. As a naturally occurring sterile hybrid it is increased only by division and shows good resistance to verticillium wilt, performing reliably in humus-rich, evenly moist woodland soil in partial to full shade. Its strongly vertical habit makes it a useful accent among lower, mounding ferns and hostas in a shaded border.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in bright shade; site out of hot afternoon sun so the golden new growth does not scorch.

directions: 'Golden Mist' wood fern produces broad, finely divided fronds whose new growth emerges a luminous golden yellow before gradually deepening to rich dark green, creating a two-toned, glowing effect through spring and early summer. Slightly larger and more openly arching than the related autumn fern, it forms an evergreen to semi-evergreen clump that holds its color and form through most winters within its hardiness range. It prefers bright shade with even moisture in humus-rich soil and shows good resistance to verticillium wilt, tolerating average garden conditions once established. Plant it where the backlit gold new fronds can be viewed against darker foliage, such as alongside hellebores or dark-leaved heucheras.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, spacing plants to allow the creeping rhizomes room to knit together into a colony over several seasons.

directions: 'Branford Rambler' is a stoloniferous hybrid between lady fern and Japanese painted fern that spreads gently by creeping rhizomes to knit together an expanding groundcover, rather than staying in a tight clump like its sibling selection 'Branford Beauty'. Upright, deciduous fronds reach about two feet tall, their fresh green blades set off by dark maroon-red stipes that echo the coloring of Japanese painted fern without the silvery variegation. It performs best in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade and is deer resistant, making it a dependable choice for massing under trees or along a shaded path. Allow room for it to ramble, or use it as a filler between larger specimen ferns and hostas where a slowly spreading textural carpet is wanted.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in fertile, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, mulching around the crown to buffer soil moisture and protect against excessive winter wet.

directions: Hard shield fern forms a classic shuttlecock-shaped rosette of stiff, glossy, dark green, bipinnate fronds with a firm, almost leathery texture that holds up well through winter in an evergreen to semi-evergreen habit. Native to woodlands and rocky slopes across Europe and temperate Asia, it prefers cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil and appreciates a mulch over the crown to buffer it from excess winter wet. In hot, humid climates such as the Gulf Coast it benefits from a coolly shaded, well-ventilated site and steady summer moisture, performing best where it is shielded from afternoon sun entirely. Its tidy, symmetrical rosette form makes an elegant specimen for a shaded rock garden or the front of a woodland border.
